query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered promising for high-heat wear-resistant use and is suitable for thin-film applications; because bulk preparation is expensive, applying it as a coating on a conventional metal is more practical. Earlier studies reported improved wear or mechanical performance from high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, and titanium-alloy substrates, and simulations of FeNiCrCoCu on Cu indicated that sliding speed affects tangential and normal forces. Other work associated composition and grain size with changes in wear damage. However, most prior studies examined a limited operating regime or the properties of the alloys themselves rather than the overall wear resistance of coatings under varied thermal conditions. Subject to retaining FeNiCrCoCu as a coating on a Cu matrix, what single intervention could improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its causal mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to an unchanged coating in matched tests, the boundaries within which it should hold, supporting evidence from the introduction, and an experiment with a clear rejection criterion for both the predicted outcome and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Grain size refinement of the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating can improve its wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a Cu matrix
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, as the evidence records do not provide a direct transferable mechanism. Grain size refinement can lead to increased hardness and wear resistance due to the Hall-Petch effect, where smaller grains can impede dislocation movement and reduce the formation of wear-induced defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating, with a reduced wear rate and coefficient of friction, compared to the unchanged coating in matched tests.
generation.baseline: Unchanged FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a Cu matrix
generation.boundary: The grain size refinement should be within the range of 100 nm to 10 μm, and the thermal and contact regimes should be within the range of 20°C to 500°C and 1 N to 100 N, respectively.
generation.uncertainty: The actual wear resistance improvement may vary depending on the specific grain size refinement method, the resulting microstructure, and the testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear tests with a Si3N4 ball on the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with refined grain size, compared to the unchanged coating, under varied thermal and contact regimes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate and coefficient of friction of the grain size refined coating are not significantly lower than those of the unchanged coating, the hypothesis is falsified.

Own digest: Paper card. Question: Can an Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating be successfully fabricated on an AZ91D magnesium alloy substrate via laser cladding to improve its wear and corrosion resistance, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating on AZ91D magnesium alloy substrate; mixed elemental powders of Cu, Ni, Al, Co, Cr, and Fe (99 wt % purity, 48–75 μm particle size). Processing: Laser cladding using a TR050 type CO2 high-power laser under 99.999% argon protection; mixed powders ball milled, preset with 4 vol % PVA solution (0.6 mm thickness); laser power 3000 W, scanning speed 10 mm/s, spot diameter 4 mm, overlap rate 25%. Test conditions: Dry sliding wear: 98 N load, 0.4187 m/s speed, 75 mins duration (1884 m distance), bearing steel (AISI52100) friction pair; Corrosion: potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt % NaCl solution, −2.5 V to 1.5 V range, 1 mV/s scan rate; Microhardness

Paper node: Frictional Wear and Corrosion Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Synthesized by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying (2020). Cited 38 times before the cutoff; 1 papers in this graph say something specific about it.
Own digest: Paper card. Question: How does the power of atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) influence the microstructure, frictional wear resistance, and corrosion resistance of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings?. System: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings (HEACs) on low carbon steel (45#) substrates. Processing: Atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using mechanically milled powders (15–50 μm) with four power levels (H1 < H2 < H3 < H4); H4 utilized the highest hydrogen-gas flow rate and power. Test conditions: Tribological tests: Si3N4 ball (5 mm), 5 N load, 1200 s sliding time; Corrosion tests: 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, room temperature, 240 h immersion, potentiodynamic polarization, EIS (100 kHz–10 MHz).
